article.title: Perilous Future of the Republic
article.author: Peter McLaren
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. American democracy is confronting a crisis that extends far beyond the personality, policies, or political ambitions of any single president. What is at stake is the historical meaning of democracy itself: whether a republic founded upon the promise of popular sovereignty can survive the concentration of executive power, the systematic weakening of institutional restraints, the mobilization of political resentment, and the transformation of public life into an arena of permanent ideological warfare. Donald Trump represents the culmination of political tendencies that have been developing within American society for decades. His presidency did not create every contradiction now confronting the republic. Rather, it has brought those contradictions into sharper relief, exposing the vulnerabilities of institutions that many Americans had assumed to be more resilient than they are. The danger is not simply that an individual president may violate democratic norms. It is that the erosion of those norms may become normalized, that the exceptional may become routine, and that the public may gradually lose the capacity to distinguish democratic government from the increasingly personalized exercise of political power. Democracy rarely disappears in a single dramatic moment. Its institutions may remain standing while their substance is hollowed out. Elections continue, courts convene, legislatures assemble, and constitutions remain ceremonially invoked. Yet the conditions necessary for meaningful democratic participation can deteriorate beneath this institutional surface. Citizens may retain the formal right to vote while losing confidence that their voices can influence the decisions shaping their lives. The question confronting the United States is therefore not merely whether its democratic institutions can withstand another political crisis. It is whether the republic can recover the social, ethical, and political commitments that make democracy something more than a procedural arrangement. The Republic at the Edge The American republic was born amid contradictions that have never been fully resolved. Its founding declarations affirmed liberty and equality while slavery remained entrenched in its economic and political foundations. The language of universal rights coexisted with the exclusion of women, Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, and those without property from the privileges of citizenship. These contradictions do not invalidate the democratic aspirations expressed in the founding documents. They reveal, rather, that democratic ideals have always exceeded the political arrangements through which they were initially articulated. The struggle for democracy has consequently involved generations of movements attempting to enlarge the meaning of freedom and extend the boundaries of political membership. The abolitionist movement, the labor movement, the women's suffrage movement, the civil rights movement, and countless struggles for economic justice have challenged the tendency of political institutions to serve the interests of established power. Democracy has advanced not simply because political elites voluntarily surrendered their privileges but because ordinary people organized to demand recognition, representation, and material change. This history matters because democracy cannot be reduced to reverence for national symbols or nostalgic appeals to an imagined golden age. A democratic republic is not democratic merely because it possesses a constitution, holds elections, or celebrates its founding documents. It must continually confront the inequalities and exclusions that undermine the promises those documents contain. The contemporary crisis emerges from the widening distance between democratic rhetoric and lived experience. Economic insecurity, declining trust in public institutions, political polarization, and the increasing influence of concentrated wealth have created conditions in which authoritarian appeals can acquire considerable force. For many Americans, political institutions appear remote, unresponsive, and incapable of addressing the difficulties of everyday life. Workers struggle to secure housing, healthcare, education, and economic stability while enormous concentrations of wealth accumulate beyond their reach. Communities experience the consequences of industrial decline, environmental destruction, and the erosion of public services. Political leaders promise renewal, yet the structures generating insecurity often remain largely intact. Authoritarian movements exploit this disillusionment. They identify enemies, promise national restoration, and present concentrated leadership as the remedy for political paralysis. They offer emotionally satisfying explanations for complicated social problems while directing public anger toward vulnerable populations, immigrants, political opponents, and supposedly disloyal citizens. The resulting politics transforms legitimate grievances into instruments of domination. The problem is not that ordinary people are incapable of democratic judgment. It is that democratic judgment becomes more difficult when public discourse is saturated with disinformation, fear, scapegoating, and the deliberate destruction of a shared factual world. A republic cannot remain healthy when citizens are encouraged to regard one another as existential enemies. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship The Imperial Presidency The American presidency has accumulated extraordinary power over the course of the nation's history. War, national security, emergency declarations, executive orders, and the expansion of administrative authority have progressively enlarged the reach of the executive branch. These developments did not begin with Trump. They reflect a longer transformation in American political life, one in which successive administrations have expanded presidential authority while Congress has frequently struggled to exercise meaningful oversight. Trump's approach to the presidency intensifies this historical tendency by treating executive power not simply as a constitutional responsibility but as an instrument of personal authority. The distinction is fundamental. A democratic president occupies an office whose legitimacy depends upon constitutional limitations, institutional accountability, and the recognition that political authority is temporary. An authoritarian leader increasingly treats those limitations as obstacles to be overcome and public institutions as instruments to be brought under personal control. Under this conception of leadership, loyalty to the president can become more important than fidelity to the law. Independent officials may be treated as enemies. Investigations may be represented as conspiracies. Judicial decisions may be denounced whenever they frustrate executive objectives. The public service itself may be reorganized around political obedience rather than professional independence. Such developments threaten the distinction between a constitutional republic and a system in which power is exercised according to the preferences of an individual leader. The danger is compounded when the president's political movement portrays any institutional resistance as illegitimate. If courts, legislatures, journalists, civil servants, and election administrators are discredited whenever they refuse to comply with executive demands, the very mechanisms designed to restrain arbitrary power become targets of political warfare. The constitutional separation of powers is not an inconvenience imposed upon effective government. It is one of the essential safeguards against the concentration of power. The founders understood that political authority requires limits because no individual, however persuasive or popular, can be presumed immune to ambition, self-interest, or the temptation to govern without restraint. The imperial presidency emerges when those limits are progressively weakened and the executive begins to behave as though the state belongs to its occupant. From Democratic Erosion to Competitive Authoritarianism Political scientists have used the concept of competitive authoritarianism to describe systems in which elections and democratic institutions continue to exist while incumbents manipulate the political environment to make genuine competition increasingly unequal. Such systems do not necessarily abolish elections. They may instead weaken the institutions that make elections meaningful: independent courts, a free press, impartial electoral administration, legislative oversight, and the ability of opposition parties to organize without intimidation. The danger for the United States is not that every feature of such systems has already become fully established. It is that democratic erosion can occur incrementally, through the cumulative weakening of safeguards that once appeared secure. An election is not sufficient to guarantee democracy. Electoral legitimacy depends upon the conditions under which political competition takes place. Citizens must be able to obtain reliable information, criticize those in power, organize collectively, and participate without fear that the machinery of government will be weaponized against them. When political leaders delegitimize electoral outcomes without credible evidence, undermine confidence in election administration, or portray political opponents as enemies of the nation, they weaken the shared commitments upon which peaceful transfers of power depend. The events surrounding January 6, 2021, demonstrated how profoundly dangerous the rejection of electoral legitimacy can become. The attack on the United States Capitol was not merely an eruption of public disorder. It was an assault upon the constitutional process through which electoral outcomes are formally recognized. The broader lesson is that democratic institutions cannot survive indefinitely when political leaders cultivate the belief that elections are legitimate only when their own side wins. Nor can democracy thrive when the public sphere becomes so saturated with conspiracy theories that evidence itself loses its authority. A political culture in which every inconvenient fact is dismissed as fabricated, every investigation is treated as persecution, and every institutional restraint is described as treason becomes increasingly incapable of resolving conflict through democratic means. The challenge is not simply to defend existing institutions. It is to restore the public trust and political culture that allow those institutions to function. Related: Che Guevara, Paulo Freire, Cuba, and the Future of Hope The Assault on Institutional Independence Democratic government requires institutions capable of exercising their responsibilities without being subordinated to the personal interests of political leaders. Courts must be able to interpret the law independently. Legislatures must be able to investigate executive conduct. Journalists must be free to scrutinize those who exercise power. Election officials must be able to administer elections without intimidation. Civil servants must be able to carry out lawful responsibilities without being forced to demonstrate personal allegiance to the president. These institutions are imperfect. They can reproduce class privilege, racial inequality, bureaucratic inertia, and other forms of injustice. Their independence does not make them immune from criticism or reform. Nevertheless, institutional independence remains essential to preventing the arbitrary exercise of political authority. The effort to subordinate public institutions to executive power represents a particularly dangerous development because it can transform the instruments of government into mechanisms of political retaliation. When public officials are threatened for performing their duties, when professional expertise is dismissed as ideological disloyalty, and when investigations are treated as unacceptable merely because they inconvenience those in power, the distinction between public service and personal obedience begins to collapse. This transformation has implications extending well beyond Washington. Universities, public schools, scientific institutions, cultural organizations, and independent media all depend upon some degree of intellectual freedom and institutional autonomy. They require the ability to examine evidence, challenge established assumptions and communicate conclusions without fear of political punishment. A society that systematically intimidates its intellectual and cultural institutions impoverishes its capacity for democratic self-understanding. The purpose of education is not to produce citizens who repeat the preferred language of those who govern them. It is to cultivate the capacity to question authority, evaluate evidence, recognize injustice, and participate thoughtfully in collective life. When these capacities are weakened, political obedience can be mistaken for civic responsibility. The defense of institutional independence must therefore be accompanied by a deeper commitment to democratic education. The Politics of Enemies Authoritarian politics depends upon the construction of enemies. Rather than acknowledging the complexity of social problems, authoritarian leaders offer narratives that divide the population into morally opposed camps. One group is presented as the authentic nation; the other is portrayed as corrupt, dangerous, parasitic, or fundamentally alien. The political leader then assumes the role of defender, promising to restore the nation by defeating those supposedly responsible for its decline. This strategy converts political disagreement into a struggle over national identity. Opponents are no longer people with different interpretations of the common good. They become enemies whose very presence is said to threaten the survival of the country. The rhetoric of national restoration can be particularly effective during periods of economic insecurity and social change. It offers a simplified account of suffering, directing anger toward identifiable targets rather than examining the economic and institutional arrangements that generate insecurity. Immigrants may be blamed for problems rooted in labor-market structures, inadequate housing, or failures of public policy. Minority populations may be portrayed as threats to social cohesion. Journalists and academics may be accused of undermining the nation simply because they challenge prevailing political narratives. Meanwhile, the power of corporations, the concentration of wealth, and the structural inequalities shaping everyday life may receive far less scrutiny. This is one of the central achievements of reactionary politics: it can mobilize genuine grievances while redirecting them away from the institutions and economic relationships that deserve critical examination. Democratic politics requires a different response. It must recognize the legitimate suffering of people whose lives have been destabilized by economic change, declining public services, and the erosion of community. Yet it must refuse the proposition that the suffering of one group can be remedied through the humiliation or exclusion of another. Solidarity does not require pretending that social conflicts do not exist. It requires understanding how those conflicts are produced and identifying possibilities for collective action that do not depend upon scapegoating. A democratic society must resist the temptation to confuse the politics of vengeance with the pursuit of justice. Related: Revolutionary Prophetic Pedagogy: Reclaiming Schools for Democracy in an Age of Oligarchy The Machinery of Power Political authority in contemporary America cannot be understood solely through the personalities of elected officials. It must also be examined in relation to the economic structures that shape the possibilities of political action. Corporate wealth, financial power, lobbying, campaign financing, media ownership, and the increasing influence of private interests over public policy all affect the conditions under which democracy operates. The formal principle of political equality becomes increasingly fragile when economic inequality translates into unequal political influence. A citizen with limited resources may possess the same legal right to vote as a billionaire, yet the two do not possess comparable opportunities to shape public debate, influence legislation, or establish the boundaries of politically acceptable discussion. This is not simply a matter of individual wealth. It concerns the institutional arrangements through which economic power becomes political power. The concentration of wealth can weaken democracy even when elections remain competitive. It can restrict the range of policies considered realistic, privilege the interests of investors over those of workers, and encourage governments to treat the demands of financial markets as more urgent than the needs of ordinary citizens. The result is a contradiction at the heart of contemporary democratic capitalism. Political systems proclaim the sovereignty of the people while economic institutions frequently organize social life according to imperatives that remain beyond meaningful democratic control. The Work of Democratic Renewal Defending American democracy requires a broad commitment to institutional accountability, civic participation, and the restoration of public trust. Independent courts, a free press, fair elections, and meaningful legislative oversight remain essential. Political leaders must be held accountable when they violate the law or attempt to undermine the constitutional responsibilities of their offices. But institutional defense alone is insufficient. Democracy also requires citizens capable of distinguishing evidence from propaganda, recognizing the historical origins of political conflict, and participating in collective deliberation without surrendering their judgment to charismatic leaders. Education consequently occupies a central position in any serious project of democratic renewal. Related: The Pedagogy of the Heart: Music, Memory, and the Pursuit of Social Justice The Republic Is Not Yet Its Future The American republic stands at a dangerous historical juncture, but its future is not predetermined. Authoritarian movements draw strength from real contradictions, unresolved injustices, and widespread disillusionment. They flourish when democratic institutions appear incapable of addressing ordinary people's needs and when political discourse becomes dominated by resentment, fear, and the search for enemies. To resist these movements effectively, democratic forces must do more than condemn their rhetoric. They must confront the conditions that make authoritarian promises attractive. They must demonstrate that democratic government can address economic insecurity, protect individual rights, strengthen public institutions, and expand opportunities for meaningful participation. They must recover the conviction that political freedom and social justice are not opposing objectives but mutually reinforcing dimensions of a genuinely democratic society. The task also requires historical honesty. American democracy has never been a completed achievement. Its history includes slavery, dispossession, exclusion, imperial ambition, and the concentration of economic power. Yet it also includes generations of people who challenged those injustices and struggled to enlarge the meaning of freedom. The democratic tradition is therefore neither an immaculate inheritance nor an irredeemable failure. It is an unfinished historical struggle whose direction depends upon the actions of those who inherit it. We must resist the temptation to regard democracy as something guaranteed by the mere survival of familiar institutions. Constitutions cannot defend themselves. Courts cannot preserve their independence without public support. Elections cannot sustain democratic legitimacy when political leaders systematically undermine the conditions of fair competition. Citizens cannot exercise meaningful freedom if they are deprived of the knowledge, resources, and collective agency necessary to participate in public life. Democracy must be continually renewed through practice. The struggle for American democracy is consequently part of a larger struggle over the future of humanity. Across the world, societies confront the concentration of wealth, ecological devastation, political polarization, technological transformation, and the growing capacity of powerful institutions to shape human life without meaningful public accountability. These challenges demand more than nostalgia for an earlier political order. They require the courage to imagine democratic possibilities that existing institutions have yet to realize. The future of the republic will depend upon whether Americans can recover the distinction between power and legitimacy, between national greatness and national domination, between political loyalty and democratic responsibility. It will depend upon whether citizens can recognize that the freedom of others is not a threat to their own, that criticism is not treason, and that the capacity to question authority is among the most important safeguards of a free society. It will depend, finally, upon whether democracy can become more than a system for selecting leaders and recover its deeper meaning as a collective commitment to human dignity, social justice, and the unfinished possibilities of historical transformation. The republic is not simply what its founders imagined, nor is it merely what its current leaders proclaim it to be. It is what successive generations make of it through their struggles, their failures, their solidarities, and their willingness to confront the contradictions of their own time. No political leader can guarantee its future. No constitution can substitute for the active participation of citizens. No appeal to national greatness can compensate for the abandonment of democratic responsibility. The struggle continues because the promise remains unfinished. The future remains unwritten. But it will not be written for us.
